learnings.title: From HTML to pixels — the render pipeline
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: The render pipeline is the fixed sequence a browser runs to turn downloaded bytes into pixels: parse HTML into a DOM, parse CSS into style rules, combine them into a render tree, lay out where everything goes, paint it, and composite the layers.

api.note: the two parse results combined; only what is actually rendered ends up here
the first is left out of the render tree entirely; the second still takes up its space
the cheap properties — they skip layout and paint and run on the compositor
the expensive ones — changing any of these re-runs layout for the whole subtree
reads that force layout to run early, before the browser was ready to

summary.useCase: Animating a sidebar with `transform: translateX()` and getting a smooth 60fps, where animating `left` drops frames because every step re-runs layout.

learnings.answer:
Everything else in this section is a detail of this one process. A browser receives bytes and has to end up with coloured pixels, and it does that in the same order every time.

![From HTML to pixels](/diagrams/webfund/render-pipeline.svg)

## The steps

1. **Bytes → characters → tokens → nodes → DOM.** The HTML parser reads top to bottom, building the DOM tree incrementally. It can paint what it has before the document is finished — this is why a slow tail of HTML does not necessarily mean a blank screen.
2. **CSS → CSSOM.** Every stylesheet is parsed into a second tree. **CSS is render-blocking**: the browser will not paint until it has the CSS it knows about, because painting first would mean showing unstyled content and repainting.
3. **DOM + CSSOM → render tree.** Only what is visible. `display: none` produces no render-tree node; `visibility: hidden` does, because it still occupies space.
4. **Layout (reflow).** Compute the geometry — the box of every node, in real pixels. This is where `%`, `em` and `auto` become numbers.
5. **Paint.** Fill in pixels for each box: text, colours, shadows, borders. Produces layers.
6. **Composite.** Assemble the layers, on the GPU where possible, and put them on screen.

## Why the order matters to you

**A `<script>` in the middle of the body stops the parser.** The DOM cannot continue being built, because the script might call `document.write`. The parser resumes only when the script has been fetched and executed — see [Script loading](/web-fundamentals/2).

**A script that reads layout must wait for CSS.** If a stylesheet is still loading, `getComputedStyle` or `offsetHeight` cannot be answered, so the script blocks until the CSSOM is ready — a script that does not even mention CSS ends up waiting on it.

**Changing a property at a different stage costs a different amount:**

| You change | Work triggered |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `top`, `font-size`, adding a node | Layout → Paint → Composite |
| `color`, `background`, `box-shadow` | Paint → Composite |
| `transform`, `opacity` | Composite only |

That table is the entire reason animations use `transform` and `opacity` rather than `left` and `width`. Sixty frames a second gives you 16.7 ms per frame; a layout pass on a large tree does not fit.

## The preload scanner

While the main parser is blocked on a script, a second, simpler parser races ahead through the raw HTML looking for `src` and `href` so it can start downloads early. It is the reason a page with a blocking script still fetches images in parallel.

It only sees **markup**. Anything discovered by JavaScript — a CSS `background-image`, a font referenced by a stylesheet the browser has not parsed yet, a lazily imported chunk — is invisible to it, which is exactly what [resource hints](/web-fundamentals/3) exist to fix.

## Reflow is not free, and you can force it

```javascript
// Layout thrashing: read, write, read, write.
for (const el of items) {
  const h = el.offsetHeight; // forces layout — the browser must flush pending writes
  el.style.height = `${h * 2}px`; // invalidates layout again
}

// Batch: all reads, then all writes. One layout.
const heights = items.map((el) => el.offsetHeight);
items.forEach((el, i) => (el.style.height = `${heights[i] * 2}px`));
```

The details of that pattern are in [Layout Thrashing & Forced Synchronous Layout](/browser/155).

## Key takeaways

- DOM and CSSOM are built separately, then combined into the render tree.
- CSS blocks rendering; a synchronous script blocks parsing — and can end up blocked on CSS.
- Layout → Paint → Composite. The property you animate decides how much of that runs.
- The preload scanner rescues markup-declared resources, not JavaScript-discovered ones.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why is CSS render-blocking but images are not?"** — Painting without CSS means a flash of unstyled content and a full [repaint](/css/6); an image can arrive later and paint into space that layout already reserved (if you gave it dimensions).
- **"What is the difference between reflow and repaint?"** — Reflow recomputes geometry, repaint refills pixels. Reflow always implies repaint; the reverse is not true.
- **"How would you make an animation cheap?"** — Keep it on `transform`/`opacity` so only the compositor runs, and promote the layer deliberately rather than by accident.

learnings.title: Script loading — blocking, async, defer and modules
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: Script loading is the choice of when a `<script>` downloads and when it runs. A plain script stops the HTML parser dead where it sits; `defer` and `async` let the parser carry on and differ in when the code finally executes.

api.note: parsing stops, downloads, runs, then parsing resumes — the slowest option
downloads alongside parsing, runs after the HTML is done, in document order — the sane default
downloads alongside parsing, runs the instant it arrives; order between async scripts is undefined
deferred automatically, so you never write `defer` on one
fires after HTML parsing and all deferred scripts — but async scripts may still be pending

summary.useCase: Moving an analytics tag from a plain `<script>` in the `<head>` to `async`, and watching first paint drop from 1.8s to 0.4s.

learnings.answer:
Where you put a `<script>` tag and which attribute you give it decides whether your page renders in 200 ms or 2 seconds. It is the highest-value thing on this page and it fits in one diagram.

![Script loading — blocking, async, defer](/diagrams/webfund/script-loading.svg)

## The four behaviours

| Form | Fetch | Execute | Parser |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `<script src>` | Immediately, blocking | The moment it arrives | **Stopped** while fetching *and* executing |
| `<script async src>` | In parallel | As soon as it lands | Paused only for execution; **order not guaranteed** |
| `<script defer src>` | In parallel | After parsing completes, before `DOMContentLoaded` | Never blocked; **document order preserved** |
| `<script type="module">` | In parallel | Deferred by default, after parsing | Like `defer`, plus its own dependency graph |

Two of those rows are the ones you use. `defer` is the sane default for your own code: it downloads in parallel, runs in order, and the DOM exists by the time it runs. `async` is right for genuinely independent third parties — an analytics beacon that touches nothing you own.

## Step through it

```trace
{
  "input": "<head> with one blocking script, one async, one defer",
  "lanes": [
    { "id": "parser", "label": "HTML parser", "kind": "slots", "slots": ["position"] },
    { "id": "tags", "label": "Scripts in the document", "kind": "cells", "cells": ["blocking.js", "async.js", "defer.js"], "indices": true },
    { "id": "log", "label": "What the browser does", "kind": "log" }
  ],
  "vars": ["parsing", "DOM ready"],
  "steps": [
    {
      "note": "The parser reaches `<script src=\"blocking.js\">`. Parsing **stops**. The preload scanner races ahead and starts the other two downloads anyway.",
      "cells": { "parser": ["at blocking.js"], "log": ["fetch blocking.js — parser stopped"] },
      "marks": { "tags": { "0": "bad" } },
      "vars": { "parsing": "stopped", "DOM ready": "no" }
    },
    {
      "note": "`blocking.js` arrives and executes. Only now can parsing resume. Every millisecond of that round trip was a millisecond of blank screen.",
      "cells": { "parser": ["at blocking.js"], "log": ["fetch blocking.js — parser stopped", "run blocking.js"] },
      "marks": { "tags": { "0": "done" } },
      "vars": { "parsing": "stopped", "DOM ready": "no" }
    },
    {
      "note": "Parsing continues. `async.js` has finished downloading, so it runs the moment it lands — interrupting the parser mid-document.",
      "cells": { "parser": ["mid-body"], "log": ["run blocking.js", "async.js landed → runs now"] },
      "marks": { "tags": { "0": "done", "1": "active" } },
      "vars": { "parsing": "interrupted", "DOM ready": "no" }
    },
    {
      "note": "Parsing finishes: the DOM is complete. `defer.js` has been waiting, downloaded, for exactly this moment.",
      "cells": { "parser": ["end of document"], "log": ["async.js ran", "parsing complete"] },
      "marks": { "tags": { "0": "done", "1": "done", "2": "window" } },
      "vars": { "parsing": "done", "DOM ready": "yes" }
    },
    {
      "note": "`defer.js` runs, in document order, with the whole DOM available — then `DOMContentLoaded` fires.",
      "cells": { "parser": ["end of document"], "log": ["parsing complete", "run defer.js", "DOMContentLoaded"] },
      "marks": { "tags": { "0": "done", "1": "done", "2": "hit" } },
      "vars": { "parsing": "done", "DOM ready": "yes" }
    }
  ]
}
```

## The rules

```html
<head>
  <!-- Your app. Parallel download, in-order execution, DOM guaranteed. -->
  <script defer src="/assets/app.8f3a2b.js"></script>

  <!-- A module is deferred already. `async` on a module opts back out. -->
  <script type="module" src="/assets/app.mjs"></script>

  <!-- Independent third party that touches nothing of yours. -->
  <script async src="https://cdn.example.com/analytics.js"></script>
</head>
```

- **`defer` for anything of yours.** In-order and DOM-ready are both things your code assumes.
- **`async` only for independent scripts.** Two `async` scripts have no ordering, so one cannot depend on the other.
- **"Put scripts at the end of the body"** is the pre-`defer` version of this advice. It still works, but `defer` in the head starts the download earlier, which is the part that mattered.
- **Inline scripts always block**, attribute or not — `async`/`defer` are ignored on them. A tiny inline script is fine; a large one is a parser stall you cannot see in the network panel.
- **`type="module"` implies deferred**, always, even inline. And modules are fetched with [CORS](/browser/156), so a cross-origin one needs `crossorigin` and the right headers.

## Common mistakes

- A blocking `<script>` in the `<head>` for a bundle that could have been `defer`.
- `async` on application code, then a race where one file runs before the library it needs.
- Assuming `defer` guarantees the *images* have loaded. It guarantees the DOM, not the subresources — that is `load`.
- A blocking third-party tag (chat widget, tag manager) in the head, which turns their outage into your blank page.

## Key takeaways

- `defer` for your code, `async` for independent third parties, plain `<script>` almost never.
- A blocking script stops the parser for the whole round trip, not just the execution.
- Modules are deferred by default and bring their own dependency graph.
- The [preload scanner](/web-fundamentals/1) keeps downloads going while the parser is stalled — but it only sees markup.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"`async` vs `defer` in one sentence?"** — Both download in parallel; `async` runs as soon as it lands and in no particular order, `defer` runs after parsing in document order.
- **"Why is `defer` in the head better than a script at the end of the body?"** — The download starts as soon as the head is parsed instead of after the whole document, and execution timing is the same.
- **"What breaks if you put `async` on your app bundle?"** — Execution can beat the DOM it queries and can reorder relative to other scripts; both are intermittent, which is the worst kind of bug.

learnings.title: Resource hints — preload, prefetch, preconnect
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: Resource hints are `<link>` tags that tell the browser about a file it will need before it would have discovered that file on its own — so the download can start early instead of waiting for the parser to reach it.

api.note: fetch now at high priority; `as` is mandatory, and fonts need `crossorigin` or you fetch twice
do the DNS, TCP and TLS handshakes now so the real fetch starts warm
just the name lookup — cheaper, and much weaker
lowest priority, for the *next* navigation, not this one
the cheaper lever: reprioritise something already in the HTML rather than preloading it

summary.useCase: A hero image inside a CSS `background-image` that the browser cannot see until the CSS parses — `preload` starts it immediately and cuts a second off Largest Contentful Paint.

learnings.answer: The browser is good at prioritising what it can *see*. Resource hints are how you tell it about the things it cannot see yet, or cannot see at all. ## The four, and what each actually does | Hint | Says | Use it for | | --- | --- | --- | | `preconnect` | "Open the connection now" — DNS + TCP + TLS, before any request | A known third-party origin you will hit soon (fonts, API, image [CDN](/system-design/115)) | | `dns-prefetch` | "Just resolve the DNS" | A fallback for `preconnect` on older browsers, or a maybe-origin | | `preload` | "Fetch this **now**, at high priority — I need it for this page" | A late-discovered critical resource: a font, a hero image, a CSS-referenced asset | | `prefetch` | "Fetch this when idle — the **next** page probably needs it" | The bundle for the route the user is most likely to click | ```html ``` ## Why preload exists at all The [preload scanner](/web-fundamentals/1) sees markup, and only markup. A font is referenced by `@font-face` inside a stylesheet, so the chain is: HTML → stylesheet → parse CSS → discover the font → fetch it. That is two full round trips of delay before the request even starts. `preload` collapses the chain by declaring the resource in the HTML where the scanner can see it immediately. The same applies to anything discovered by JavaScript: a hero image set via `background-image`, a chunk imported inside a click handler, a JSON payload your app fetches on boot. ## `fetchpriority`, the cheaper lever ```html ``` Images below the fold are fetched at low priority automatically, but the browser cannot know which of three above-the-fold images is the LCP element. `fetchpriority="high"` on that one, and `loading="lazy"` on everything below the fold, usually beats adding another `preload`. ## The rules that keep hints from backfiring - **`preload` is a promise you have to keep.** If nothing uses the resource within a few seconds, the console warns and you have spent bandwidth competing with resources that mattered. - **Preloading everything is preloading nothing.** Hints work by reordering a queue; move everything to the front and the order is unchanged, minus the bandwidth you wasted. - **`as` is mandatory.** Without it the browser cannot assign a priority or match the eventual request, and the resource is fetched twice. - **`crossorigin` must match the eventual request exactly.** Fonts are always fetched in [CORS](/browser/156) mode, so a font `preload` without `crossorigin` is a guaranteed double download — the classic version of this bug. - **Four to six `preconnect`s at most.** Each one holds an open connection; beyond a handful they contend for bandwidth with the requests you actually made. ## Key takeaways - `preconnect` buys the handshake, `preload` buys the round trips to discovery, `prefetch` buys the *next* navigation. - Preload is for late-discovered critical resources, above all fonts and the LCP image. - Get `as` and `crossorigin` right or you download the file twice. - `fetchpriority` and `loading="lazy"` are often the cheaper fix. ## Interview follow-ups - **"`preload` vs `prefetch`?"** — Priority and intent: preload is "this page needs it now", prefetch is "the next page might, do it when idle". - **"Why does a preloaded font sometimes download twice?"** — A `crossorigin` mismatch, so the preloaded response does not match the CSS-issued request and cannot be reused. - **"When would you not add a hint?"** — When the resource is already discoverable in the markup at the right priority; the hint then only adds contention.

learnings.title: The document head — what belongs there and in what order
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: The `<head>` is read top to bottom by a parser that halts for some of its contents, so the order of the tags in it is a schedule, not a style preference — what you put first decides what downloads first.

api.note: first, within the first 1024 bytes, or the parser may have to restart
next — mobile layout depends on it, and it costs nothing
early, so the handshakes to third-party origins run while the rest parses
render-blocking — before it, nothing paints; after it, everything is already waiting
loads without blocking render — the trick for non-critical CSS
not in the head, but the thing most often missing — screen readers pick the wrong voice without it

summary.useCase: A `<title>` placed above the stylesheet so the tab label appears immediately, instead of the tab sitting blank while a 200 kB CSS file downloads.

learnings.answer:
The `<head>` is executed top to bottom by a parser that stops for some of it. Order is not cosmetic — it is a schedule.

## The order that works

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- 1. Encoding, first, within the first 1024 bytes.
         Otherwise the parser guesses and may restart. -->
    <meta charset="utf-8" />

    <!-- 2. Viewport, before any CSS — layout depends on it. -->
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />

    <!-- 3. Title, early: it is what the tab and the crawler read first. -->
    <title>Page title — Site</title>

    <!-- 4. Connections to origins you are about to use. -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />

    <!-- 5. Critical CSS, or the stylesheet link. Render-blocking, on purpose. -->
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.8f3a.css" />

    <!-- 6. Preloads for late-discovered critical resources. -->
    <link
      rel="preload"
      as="font"
      type="font/woff2"
      href="/fonts/inter.woff2"
      crossorigin
    />

    <!-- 7. Scripts, deferred. -->
    <script defer src="/assets/app.2b7c.js"></script>

    <!-- 8. Everything that does not affect the first paint. -->
    <meta name="description" content="…" />
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/page" />
    <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml" />
  </head>
</html>
```

## Why each position

- **`charset` first.** The parser needs the encoding before it can interpret bytes as characters. Declared late, it may throw away its work and re-parse.
- **`viewport` before CSS.** Media queries and layout depend on the viewport width; setting it after the stylesheet can cost a re-layout.
- **CSS before scripts.** A script that reads layout blocks until the [CSSOM](/web-fundamentals/1) is ready; putting the stylesheet first means that wait overlaps with the script's own download instead of following it.
- **`preconnect` before the request that needs it**, or it saves nothing.
- **Everything social and descriptive last.** `og:` tags, canonical, icons — a crawler reads the whole head, and none of it affects the first paint.

## The bits people get wrong

- **A blocking `<script>` above the stylesheet.** Now nothing is downloading the CSS during that script's round trip.
- **A synchronous third-party tag in the head.** Their latency becomes your Time to First Byte, and their outage becomes your blank page.
- **Multiple stylesheets, all render-blocking.** They are fetched in parallel but paint waits for the last one. Split by media (`media="print"`) or inline the critical part.
- **`title` after 40 lines of meta tags.** Not a performance bug, but the first thing a person sees in the tab.
- **No `lang` on `<html>`.** Screen readers pick the wrong voice, and hyphenation rules go with it.

## Non-blocking CSS, when you need it

```html
<!-- Load a non-critical stylesheet without blocking the first paint. -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print" />
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="/below-the-fold.css"
  media="print"
  onload="this.media = 'all'"
/>
```

The `media="print"` trick downloads at low priority without blocking render, then swaps to `all` once it has arrived. Use it sparingly — a late stylesheet swap can cause a visible [reflow](/css/6).

## Key takeaways

- `charset`, `viewport`, `title`, connections, CSS, preloads, deferred scripts, then the rest.
- Anything render-blocking should be as early and as small as possible.
- A third-party script in the head makes their uptime your uptime.
- `lang` on `<html>` is one attribute and it is an accessibility requirement.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why must `charset` come first?"** — The parser has to know how to decode bytes; discovering it late can force a re-parse of everything it has read.
- **"How would you stop a stylesheet blocking the first paint?"** — Inline the critical rules and load the rest with the `media` swap, or split the stylesheet by route.

learnings.title: How CSS is actually applied — cascade, inheritance, computed values
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: Three separate mechanisms decide what a CSS property ends up as: the cascade picks which declaration wins, inheritance fills in anything you never declared, and the value is then resolved through several stages before it is used.

api.signature: cascade order: layer → specificity → source order
api.note: origin and `@layer` come first — specificity only breaks ties inside the same layer
counted as a tuple, not a score — one id always beats any number of classes
specificity zero, which is how you write a default that is trivially overridden
jumps the whole ordering; in `@layer` the importance order is *reversed*
the four explicit value keywords — `revert` goes back to the browser's stylesheet, `initial` to the spec default
inherits and resolves at use time, so it is substituted late and cannot be transitioned like a normal value

summary.useCase: A button that ignores your class because a `#sidebar a` rule elsewhere has one id in it — no amount of extra classes wins, and wrapping the other rule in `:where()` does.

learnings.answer:
Most "CSS is weird" moments are one of three mechanisms being invisible: the cascade choosing a declaration, inheritance filling in what you did not declare, and the value being resolved through several stages before it becomes pixels.

## The cascade, in the real order

For one property on one element, the browser sorts every declaration that matches and takes the winner. In order of precedence:

1. **Origin and importance** — user-agent < user < author < author `!important` < user `!important`. `!important` genuinely inverts the order, which is why it is so hard to undo.
2. **Cascade layers** (`@layer`) — an unlayered declaration beats a layered one, and later layers beat earlier ones.
3. **Specificity** — `(inline, id, class/attribute/pseudo-class, element)`, compared left to right. Detail and examples: [CSS Specificity and Selector Priority](/css/3).
4. **Source order** — the last one wins. This is the tie-break, not the rule.

```css
@layer reset, components, utilities;

@layer components {
  .button { padding: 8px 16px; }   /* loses to anything in utilities… */
}
@layer utilities {
  .p-0 { padding: 0; }             /* …regardless of specificity */
}
```

Layers are the modern answer to the specificity arms race: instead of adding another class to win, you declare *which bucket wins* once, and the selectors inside stay simple.

`:where()` is the other half — it has **zero specificity**, so `:where(.a, .b) p` is as easy to override as `p`.

## Inheritance

Some properties inherit by default (`color`, `font-*`, `line-height`, `visibility`, `cursor`); most do not (`margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`, `display`). That split is why setting `font-family` on `body` styles the whole page but setting `border` there does not.

Four keywords control it explicitly:

| Keyword | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `inherit` | Take the parent's computed value, always |
| `initial` | The property's spec default — **not** the browser's stylesheet value |
| `unset` | `inherit` for inheriting properties, `initial` for the rest |
| `revert` | Roll back to the previous origin — usually the browser's own stylesheet |

`initial` on `display` is `inline`, not `block` — a common surprise. `revert` is usually what people actually mean.

## The value stages

One declared value passes through several forms before layout:

```
specified  →  computed  →  used  →  actual
font-size: 2em     32px        32px      32px
width: 50%         50%         640px     640px
```

- **Computed** resolves relative units against the element and is what inherits — this is why a child of a `font-size: 2em` parent doubles again, and why `line-height: 1.5` (unitless) inherits the *ratio* while `line-height: 150%` inherits the *result*.
- **Used** needs layout: percentages and `auto` become real pixels only once the containing block is known.
- **Actual** is the used value after the device rounds it.

`getComputedStyle()` returns the *resolved* value, which is the used value for layout properties and the computed value for the rest — which is why it can force a layout pass ([layout thrashing](/browser/155)).

## Custom properties are different

```css
:root { --gap: 8px; }
.card { --gap: 16px; padding: var(--gap); } /* 16px, and children inherit 16px */
```

Custom properties **inherit** and are resolved at computed-value time, so a variable set on an ancestor changes every descendant that reads it — no rebuild, no re-declaration. That is what makes them the right vehicle for theming, and why the app's own design tokens work that way.

## Key takeaways

- Importance → layers → specificity → source order. Specificity is one step, not the whole story.
- `@layer` and `:where()` are how you stop competing on specificity.
- Inherited vs non-inherited is a fixed property list; `unset` and `revert` are the escape hatches.
- Computed values inherit; used values need layout. Unitless `line-height` inherits the ratio.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you override a third-party style without `!important`?"** — Put your rules in a later `@layer`, or reduce theirs with `:where()` if you control the import.
- **"Why does `line-height: 1.5` behave differently from `150%`?"** — The unitless version inherits the ratio and recomputes per element; the percentage inherits the already-computed pixel value.
- **"What does `getComputedStyle` cost?"** — For a layout property it forces the browser to flush pending style and layout work before it can answer.

learnings.title: Web fonts — FOIT, FOUT, font-display and subsetting
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: A web font is a font file your CSS downloads. It arrives late — the browser only learns it is needed after the CSS has parsed and it has found text that uses it — so your text is either invisible or in the wrong font until it lands.

api.note: show a fallback immediately and swap when the font lands — flash of unstyled text, no invisible text
one short window; if the font misses it, the fallback stays for this page load — no shift at all
start the download before the CSS reveals it; `crossorigin` is required even for your own domain
match the fallback's metrics to the real font so the swap does not move the text
subsetting: ship only the glyphs the page uses, often a 10× saving
the only format worth serving now; the old `ttf`/`eot` fallback stack is dead weight

summary.useCase: A heading that is invisible for 800ms on a slow connection, fixed by one line — `font-display: swap` — so it renders in a system font and swaps when the webfont lands.

learnings.title: Images — formats, srcset, lazy loading and CLS
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: Images are usually the heaviest thing a page downloads and the most common cause of content jumping around as it loads. Three declarative HTML features handle nearly all of it: the right format, the right size for the screen, and reserved space.

api.note: lets the browser reserve the box before the file arrives — the single fix for image layout shift
the CSS equivalent when the image is fluid; keeps the reserved box the right shape
offer several widths and say how wide the slot is, so the browser picks one file
for changing *format* or art direction — a different crop on mobile
defer offscreen images; never put it on the hero, which is the one you need first
on the hero image, to pull it ahead of everything else in the queue

summary.useCase: An article where the text jumps down as each photo loads — adding `width` and `height` to every `` reserves the space up front and the jumping stops.

learnings.answer: Images are usually the largest thing you ship and the most common cause of layout shift. Three declarative features cover nearly all of it. ## Formats, in one table | Format | Use for | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | **AVIF** | Photos | Smallest, ~50% under JPEG; slower to encode | | **WebP** | Photos, everything | ~30% under JPEG, universally supported | | **JPEG** | The fallback | Still fine; use progressive | | **PNG** | Transparency, screenshots, flat colour | Lossless and large — never for photos | | **SVG** | Icons, logos, diagrams | Scales, themeable via CSS if inlined | ```html ``` The browser takes the first `` it understands. `` is the fallback and carries the attributes. ## Responsive images ```html ``` - **`srcset` with `w` descriptors** tells the browser what each file *is*, in real pixels. - **`sizes`** tells it how big the image will be *rendered* — the browser cannot know before layout, and it chooses the file before layout. Getting `sizes` wrong is why the browser downloads a 1600px file for a 300px slot. - The browser also accounts for device pixel ratio, so you do not write `2x` variants by hand. ## Stop the layout shift **Always set `width` and `height`.** Modern browsers turn them into an `aspect-ratio`, reserving the correct box before a single byte of the image arrives. Without them, the image occupies zero height, everything below it renders, then jumps down when the image lands — Cumulative Layout Shift, and the most common source of it. ```css img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } /* keeps the attributes responsive */ ``` For a container whose ratio is fixed but whose image size is not: ```css .thumb { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; } ``` ## Lazy loading and priority ```html ``` - **Never `loading="lazy"` on the LCP image.** It delays the request past layout and directly regresses your headline metric — a top-three self-inflicted performance bug. - `decoding="async"` keeps the decode off the critical path. - Below-the-fold images are already deprioritised by the browser; `lazy` additionally skips them entirely until they approach the viewport. ## Alt text, briefly - Informative image: describe what it conveys, not what it depicts pixel by pixel. - Decorative image: `alt=""` — empty, present. Omitting the attribute makes a [screen reader](/system-design/406) read the filename. - An image inside a link: the alt text describes the *destination*, because that is what it acts as. ## Key takeaways - AVIF/WebP with a JPEG fallback via ``; SVG for anything vector. - `srcset` + `sizes` so the browser picks the file; wrong `sizes` is the usual cause of oversized downloads. - `width` and `height` on every image — that is the CLS fix. - `loading="lazy"` below the fold, never on the LCP image. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do you fix layout shift from images?"** — Intrinsic dimensions or `aspect-ratio`, so the box exists before the bytes do. - **"`srcset` vs ``?"** — `srcset` is the same image at different sizes and the browser chooses; `` is *art direction* or format negotiation and you choose. - **"Your LCP is 4 s and it is a hero image."** — Check that it is not lazy-loaded, is preloaded or `fetchpriority="high"`, is AVIF/WebP, is sized for the slot, and is served from a [CDN](/system-design/115) close to the user.

learnings.title: What a bundler actually does
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: A bundler is the tool that takes your entry file, follows every import to build a graph of your code, transforms each file, and writes out the small number of files the browser actually downloads.

api.note: job one: turn every import string into a real file on disk, including bare `react`
job two: TypeScript, JSX and modern syntax down to something browsers run
job three: walk every import from the entry, which is what makes tree shaking possible
job four: split the graph into files; each dynamic `import()` becomes a split point
the fields resolution actually reads, and where most "it works in dev but not the build" bugs live
swapped at build time, which is how the whole development branch of a library disappears

summary.useCase: A dev server that starts in 200ms but a production build that takes two minutes — they are doing different jobs, and only the second one bundles.

learnings.answer:
"It bundles" explains nothing. A bundler runs four distinct jobs, and every configuration question you have is really a question about one of them.

![What a bundler does — resolve, transform, graph, emit](/diagrams/webfund/bundler-pipeline.svg)

## The four jobs

**1 · Resolve.** Turn a specifier into a file. `./utils` → `./utils.ts`; `react` → `node_modules/react/index.js`, chosen by the `exports` map, the `main`/`module` fields and the current condition (`import` vs `require`, `browser` vs `node`, `development` vs `production`). Nearly every "module not found" is a resolution problem, not a bundling one.

**2 · Transform.** Run each file through a loader: TypeScript stripped, JSX compiled, CSS extracted or turned into a module, an SVG into a component, syntax lowered to the browser targets. Historically Babel; now usually esbuild or SWC, which is where most of the speed jump of the last few years came from.

**3 · Build the graph.** Start at the entry, follow every static `import`, mark every `import()` as a **split point**. The result is a directed graph of modules with the dynamic boundaries marked.

**4 · Emit.** Cut the graph into chunks, order them, minify, hash the filenames for cache busting, and write a manifest so the HTML knows what to load.

```javascript
// vite.config.js — the two knobs you actually turn.
export default {
  build: {
    target: "es2020", // job 2: how far to lower
    rollupOptions: {
      output: {
        manualChunks: {
          // job 4: chunk by change frequency
          react: ["react", "react-dom"],
        },
      },
    },
  },
};
```

## Dev server vs production build

They are two different programs, and expecting them to behave identically is a common source of "works in dev, broken in prod".

| | Dev (Vite) | Production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modules | Served native ESM, unbundled | Bundled and chunked |
| Transform | On demand, per file | Whole graph |
| Dependencies | Pre-bundled once with esbuild | Bundled with the app |
| Minify / tree-shake | No | Yes |
| Source maps | Cheap | Configured |

[Tree shaking](/web-fundamentals/10), minification and chunking only happen in the production build — which is why a bug caused by a side effect being dropped never reproduces locally.

## Chunking, briefly

Split by **change frequency**, not by folder: framework, vendor, shared, per-route. A deploy should invalidate the smallest possible surface. The full argument, with the caching headers that make it work, is in [Build and deploy topology](/system-design/109).

Two failure modes:
- **Too few chunks** — every deploy re-downloads everything.
- **Too many** — dozens of tiny requests, and on HTTP/1.1 a connection limit; even on [HTTP/2](/browser/161) each chunk has its own compression floor and execution overhead.

## The tools, and when each fits

| Tool | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| **Vite** | Dev server on native ESM + Rollup for production. The default for apps. |
| **esbuild** | Go, extremely fast, used *inside* other tools. Fewer plugins. |
| **Rollup** | The library bundler: cleanest ESM output, best tree shaking. |
| **webpack** | The most configurable and the most established; slower, huge plugin ecosystem. |
| **Rspack / Turbopack** | Rust rewrites of the webpack model, aimed at large existing configs. |

For an app: Vite. For a published library: Rollup (or tsup over esbuild). For a legacy monolith with 40 plugins: webpack, until someone funds the migration.

## Key takeaways

- Resolve → transform → graph → emit. Name the stage and the problem gets much smaller.
- `import()` is what creates a chunk boundary; nothing else does.
- Dev and production are different pipelines — tree shaking and minification are production-only.
- Chunk by change frequency so a deploy invalidates as little as possible.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why is the dev server so fast now?"** — It does not bundle: it serves native ESM and transforms each file on request, with dependencies pre-bundled once.
- **"How do you decide chunk boundaries?"** — Route-level `import()` first, then split by how often each group changes, then measure against a size budget in CI.
- **"Something works in dev and breaks in the build."** — Almost always tree shaking removing a side effect, a different resolution condition, or minification exposing a reliance on function names.

learnings.title: Tree shaking — and why it silently fails
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: Tree shaking is the bundler removing code you never use. It walks out from the entry file, marks everything reachable, and drops the rest — but only where it can prove that dropping the code changes nothing observable.

api.note: in package.json: your promise that importing a file does nothing on its own, so unused ones can go
the honest version — CSS imports do have an effect and must be kept
the classic silent failure: one import from the barrel can pull in every module behind it
a computed member access is unprovable, so nothing in that namespace can be dropped
annotate a call whose result is unused as safe to delete
verify rather than assume — the only way to know whether it worked

summary.useCase: Importing one icon from a library and finding all 900 in your bundle, because the package is a barrel file with no `sideEffects` declaration.

learnings.answer:
Tree shaking is dead-code elimination over the module graph: keep what is reachable from the entry, drop the rest. It works only when the [bundler](/web-fundamentals/9) can *prove* that dropping something changes nothing — and most of the time it cannot.

## What must be true

1. **ESM.** Static imports and exports, so the graph is known without running the code ([ESM vs CJS](/web-fundamentals/8)).
2. **Production build.** It does not run in dev.
3. **No side effects** — or an honest declaration of where they are.

## The side-effect problem

A module's top level can do things: register a polyfill, add a global, inject CSS. A bundler that drops an unused import from such a module breaks the app. So unless told otherwise, it keeps the whole module.

```json
// package.json — "importing my modules changes nothing on its own"
{ "sideEffects": false }

// Or, honestly, the ones that do:
{ "sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"] }
```

`"sideEffects": false` on a package whose CSS import you rely on will silently delete your styles. It is a promise, and it must be true.

```javascript
// This is a side effect, and it defeats shaking for the whole module.
window.myLib = createLib();

// So is this — the call happens at import time.
export const config = loadConfig();

// This is not: nothing runs until someone calls it.
export const createConfig = () => loadConfig();
```

## Barrel files

```javascript
// components/index.js — the barrel
export * from "./Button";
export * from "./Table";
export * from "./Chart"; // pulls in a 180 kB charting library

// Somewhere else
import { Button } from "../components"; // did you just import the chart library?
```

Ideally the bundler shakes the rest away. In practice it often cannot: one re-exported module has a side effect, or a CJS dependency sits in the chain, or the analysis gives up on a deep `export *`. The barrel also hurts dev-server speed and cold builds, because every consumer pulls the whole index.

Import from the file, not the barrel — `import { Button } from "../components/Button"` — or keep barrels to leaf-level, side-effect-free modules.

## The other silent failures

- **A CommonJS dependency.** Its exports are dynamic, so the interop wrapper keeps the whole file. Prefer packages that ship an ESM build.
- **Class methods.** Minifiers rarely drop unused methods on a class, because a property access could reach any of them. A tree of small functions shakes; a large class does not.
- **`import * as X`.** Namespace imports are shakeable in principle, but a single dynamic access (`X[name]`) forces everything to be kept.
- **Polyfills and `core-js`.** Imported for effect, by design. Target modern browsers and ship fewer of them.
- **`/*#__PURE__*/` missing.** A top-level function call the bundler cannot prove is pure is kept. Library authors annotate; app authors should avoid top-level calls.

## Verify, do not assume

```bash
npx vite-bundle-visualizer          # or rollup-plugin-visualizer / webpack-bundle-analyzer
```

Open the treemap and look for the module you thought you shook out. A size budget that fails CI is the guard that keeps it out later — see [Build and deploy topology](/system-design/109).

## Key takeaways

- Tree shaking needs ESM, a production build, and provable absence of side effects.
- `sideEffects` in `package.json` is the single most load-bearing flag, in both directions.
- Barrel files, CJS dependencies and large classes are the three usual reasons nothing was shaken.
- Measure with a bundle visualiser; "it should be tree-shaken" is not evidence.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why did importing one icon add 300 kB?"** — A barrel re-exporting the whole set, over a package with no `sideEffects` declaration or a CJS build.
- **"What is a side effect for a bundler?"** — Anything a module does at import time that is observable outside it: assigning a global, registering, injecting CSS, calling a function at the top level.
- **"How would you prove a dependency was dropped?"** — Bundle analyser on the production build, plus a size budget in CI so it stays dropped.

learnings.title: Forms — labels, validation, and what actually submits
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: A form is the browser's own data-collection widget. It already knows how to label fields, validate them, show the right mobile keyboard, autofill them and submit them — most form bugs come from replacing that behaviour rather than using it.

api.note: the name of the field; without it the input is unlabelled to a screen reader and the text is not clickable
what actually gets submitted — a field with no `name` is not in the payload at all
changes the mobile keyboard and gets you free validation
the specific tokens password managers look for; `off` is mostly ignored and mostly wrong
style the error state only *after* the user has interacted — unlike `:invalid`, which is red from the start
read every named field at once, instead of one controlled state hook per input

summary.useCase: A checkout where mobile users get the full alphabet keyboard for their card number — `inputmode="numeric"` and the right `autocomplete` token fix it without any JavaScript.

learnings.answer:
Forms are where the platform gives you the most for free and where frameworks most often throw it away.

## The label is not optional

```html
<!-- Explicit: for → id. Works everywhere, and clicking the text focuses the input. -->
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required />

<!-- Implicit: wrapping. Fine, but harder to style. -->
<label>Email <input name="email" type="email" /></label>
```

A placeholder is **not** a label: it disappears on focus, fails contrast in most designs, and is announced inconsistently. `aria-label` is the fallback for a genuinely label-less control (a search field with an icon), not the default.

`name` is what appears in the submitted data. An input without `name` submits nothing — the single most common "why is the field missing on the server".

## Input types earn their keep on mobile

`type="email"`, `tel`, `url`, `number`, `date`, `search` change the on-screen keyboard, add free validation, and enable the right autofill. Pair them with `autocomplete` (`email`, `current-password`, `new-password`, `one-time-code`, `street-address`) — filling a checkout by hand is a conversion problem, and `autocomplete="off"` on an address form is user-hostile.

Use `inputmode="numeric"` for a numeric string like an OTP; `type="number"` on a card number gives you spinners and a value that drops leading zeros.

## Native validation, and where it stops

```html
<input
  type="email"
  required
  minlength="3"
  maxlength="80"
  pattern="[^@]+@[^@]+"
/>
```

```javascript
form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  if (!form.checkValidity()) {
    event.preventDefault();
    // Show your own messages; the browser bubbles are unstyleable and vanish.
    for (const field of form.elements) {
      if (field.willValidate && !field.checkValidity())
        showError(field, field.validationMessage);
    }
  }
});

// A custom rule joins the same system rather than living beside it.
confirm.addEventListener("input", () => {
  confirm.setCustomValidity(
    confirm.value === password.value ? "" : "Passwords do not match",
  );
});
```

`novalidate` on the `<form>` turns off the browser's UI while keeping the API — the usual setup for a custom design. And `:user-invalid` styles a field only *after* the user has interacted with it, which is what you actually want instead of `:invalid` painting every empty required field red on load.

**Server-side validation is not optional.** Everything above is UX; the request can be made without the page.

## Submission

```javascript
form.addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = new FormData(form); // every named control, files included
  data.append("source", "settings-page");

  await fetch("/api/profile", { method: "POST", body: data }); // multipart, no header needed
  // JSON instead: JSON.stringify(Object.fromEntries(data))
});
```

Things worth knowing:

- A `<button>` inside a form is `type="submit"` **by default**. A button that does something else needs `type="button"` — otherwise it submits the form and reloads the page.
- Enter in a text input submits the form via the first submit button. Removing that button breaks Enter for keyboard users.
- Disabled controls do not submit. Use `readonly` when you still want the value.
- Checkbox groups: repeat `name`, read with `data.getAll(name)`.
- Multiple submit buttons: give each a `name`/`value` to tell them apart server-side.

## Errors people can actually use

- Put the message **next to the field**, and connect it: `aria-describedby="email-error"` plus `aria-invalid="true"`.
- Summarise at the top for long forms, with links to each field.
- Announce asynchronous errors with an `aria-live="polite"` region, or focus moves nowhere and a [screen reader](/system-design/406) user hears nothing.
- Never clear what the user typed on a failed submit.
- Validate on blur and on submit, not on every keystroke — mid-typing errors are noise.

## Controlled vs uncontrolled, briefly

React's controlled input re-renders on every keystroke and gives you per-key control; an uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM and you read it with `FormData` on submit. For a large form, uncontrolled plus native validation is usually both faster and less code — see [Controlled vs. Uncontrolled](/react-guide/22) for the React-side trade-off.

## Key takeaways

- Label every control, and give it a `name` — that is what submits.
- Input types and `autocomplete` are the mobile experience.
- Use the constraint validation API and style with `:user-invalid`; the browser's own bubbles are not designable.
- `FormData` handles multipart and files without you touching a header.
- Errors belong beside the field, wired up with `aria-describedby`.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why is placeholder not a label?"** — It vanishes on focus, is often too low-contrast, and is not reliably announced. The user loses the question while answering it.
- **"How do you validate?"** — Native constraints for the common rules, `setCustomValidity` for the rest, `novalidate` so the UI is mine, and the server as the actual authority.
- **"Your form reloads the page when a button is clicked."** — The button defaulted to `type="submit"`.

learnings.title: CSS layout — flow, flex and grid
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: CSS has three layout systems. Flow is the default — blocks stack, text wraps. Flex lays things out along one axis. Grid lays them out on two at once. Most layout arguments are really about which of the three the problem belongs to.

api.note: equal columns regardless of content; `flex: auto` is `1 1 auto`, which sizes by content instead
the fix for a flex child that refuses to shrink — the default `min-width: auto` is the culprit
the grid version of the same problem, for a track that overflows its content
a responsive grid with no media queries at all; `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks
two lines to centre anything in both directions
respond to the component's own width rather than the viewport's

summary.useCase: A card whose long unbroken title stretches the flex row and pushes the price offscreen — one `min-width: 0` on the text column and it wraps instead.

learnings.answer:
Three layout systems, and almost every layout argument is really a disagreement about which one the problem belongs to.

![Flow, flex and grid — the same content in three systems](/diagrams/webfund/layout-systems.svg)

## Which one, in one line each

| System | Shape of problem | Sizing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Flow** | A document: text, headings, paragraphs | Block fills the inline axis, height from content |
| **Flex** | One axis — a row or a column of items | Content-out: items size themselves, then distribute |
| **Grid** | Two axes at once — rows *and* columns aligned | Container-in: you define the tracks, items land in them |

The useful test: **do the items in the other direction have to line up?** A toolbar, a list of chips, a card footer — no, that is flex. A page shell, a form with aligned label and field columns, a photo gallery — yes, that is grid.

Nesting them is normal: a grid page shell whose header is a flex row.

## Flow is still doing most of the work

Before either of the other two: block boxes stack, inline boxes flow, and the box model decides the numbers.

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; } /* width includes padding + border */
```

Two flow behaviours that surprise people:

- **Margin collapse.** Adjacent vertical margins merge into the larger one, and a parent with no padding or border collapses with its first child. It does not happen in flex or grid, which is half of why people reach for them.
- **Containing block.** A percentage width resolves against the containing block, and `position: absolute` resolves against the nearest positioned ancestor — not the parent.

## Flex, the parts that matter

```css
.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  gap: 12px;              /* replaces margin hacks entirely */
  align-items: center;    /* cross axis */
  justify-content: space-between; /* main axis */
  flex-wrap: wrap;        /* let it break rather than overflow */
}
.toolbar .spacer { margin-inline-start: auto; } /* push the rest to the end */
```

`flex: 1` is shorthand for `1 1 0%` — grow, shrink, ignore my content width — which is why sidebars end up equal instead of proportional. `flex: auto` (`1 1 auto`) starts from the content size. `min-width: 0` on a flex child is the fix for the classic "text refuses to truncate": the default `min-width: auto` will not shrink below the content.

## Grid, the parts that matter

```css
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(200px, 260px) 1fr;  /* sidebar, content */
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  min-height: 100dvh;
}

/* A responsive gallery with no media queries at all. */
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}
```

`auto-fit` vs `auto-fill`: `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks so the existing items stretch; `auto-fill` keeps them, so items stay their size. `1fr` means "one share of the *leftover* space", and `minmax(0, 1fr)` is the grid version of the truncation fix.

Named areas make an intent obvious in review:

```css
.app {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas: "nav header" "nav main";
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
}
.app > nav { grid-area: nav; }
```

## Centring, and the modern conveniences

Centring is [its own entry](/css/2); the two-line version is `display: grid; place-items: center;`. Worth knowing alongside it:

- **Container queries** — `container-type: inline-size` plus `@container (min-width: 400px)`. A component that responds to *its own* width is what people wanted media queries to be.
- **Logical properties** — `margin-inline`, `padding-block`, `inset`. They flip correctly in RTL, which the physical ones do not.
- **`aspect-ratio`**, `min()`, `max()`, `clamp()` — `font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem)` replaces three breakpoints.
- **Subgrid** — a child's tracks align with the parent's, which is how you finally align card contents across a row.

## Key takeaways

- Flow for documents, flex for one axis, grid when both axes must align.
- `gap` everywhere; `min-width: 0` / `minmax(0, 1fr)` when content refuses to shrink.
- `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks, `auto-fill` keeps them.
- Container queries and logical properties are the two modern defaults worth adopting now.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Flex or grid for a card layout?"** — Grid if rows must align across cards; flex if it is a single wrapping row where alignment between rows does not matter.
- **"Why won't my flex text truncate?"** — `min-width: auto` on the flex item; set `min-width: 0`.
- **"How do you build a responsive gallery without media queries?"** — `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr))`, and container queries where the component's own width is what matters.

learnings.title: fetch, streams and AbortController
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: `fetch` makes an HTTP request and returns a promise. Three of its behaviours surprise people: it does not reject on a 404 or 500, the response body is a stream you can only read once, and it has no timeout of its own.

api.note: the check you must write — only a network failure rejects, and that throws a bare `TypeError`
each consumes the body; a second call on the same response throws
when you genuinely need to read it twice, for example to log and to parse
cancellation; the same signal also works with `addEventListener(…, { signal })`

cookies are not sent cross-origin without it — the commonest "my session is missing" bug

learnings.title: Service workers and offline
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: A service worker is a proxy you write in JavaScript. It runs in its own thread between your page and the network, sees every request the page makes, and can answer from a cache instead of going to the server — which is what makes a site work offline.

api.note: installs it; it controls pages within its scope, which defaults to the folder the file sits in
the lifecycle; a new worker waits until every old tab is gone, which is why your update does not appear
skip that wait and take control immediately — use knowingly, it can mix old and new assets
the interception point: return your own `Response` and the network is never touched
precache the app shell during install, so the first offline load has something to show
delete old cache names, or users are served last month's build forever

summary.useCase: A field app that has to keep working in a warehouse with no signal — the shell and the last data load come from the cache, and writes queue until the connection returns.

learnings.title: Where to put data in the browser
learnings.source: user request: web fundamentals every frontend engineer needs

summary.definition: The browser gives you about six places to keep data, and the choice comes down to three questions: does the server need to see it, does it have to survive a reload, and is it secret?

api.note: strings, survives restarts, per-origin — and synchronous, so a big write blocks the main thread
same API, per-tab, gone when the tab closes
the only option the server sees automatically, and the only one script cannot read
asynchronous, structured, large — worth it for real datasets, and worth a wrapper like `idb`
whole `Response` objects, for the service worker to serve back
the right answer more often than people think — an access token that must not outlive the tab

summary.useCase: Storing `undefined` in `localStorage` and getting the string `"undefined"` back on reload, which then crashes `JSON.parse` — the API only ever stores strings.
